cues.text: Imagine three users connect to your server at the same time—yet your server runs on only one CPU thread.
In a blocking server, User A's slow five-second LLM call locks that single thread, forcing User B's quick ping and User C's database query to wait sequentially in line.

With async, we still use just one CPU thread. When User A hits await, Python saves User A's paused line number and local variables into a one-kilobyte coroutine frame in RAM, freeing the CPU immediately.
Now free, that exact same thread finishes User B's fast ping first, and starts User C's database query—so requests complete by speed, not arrival order.

Notice that the database and LLM never touch RAM directly. When the database finishes first, its reply arrives at an OS socket, waking the CPU, which pulls Coroutine C down from RAM—and later does the same for User A.

This matters even when you are the only human user. After the LLM asks permission to run a tool, your chat coroutine parks in RAM waiting on an approval flag—leaving the CPU free to catch your approve click and wake that coroutine up.

Under the hood, your network card copies simultaneous bytes straight to RAM via DMA while OS kernel epoll or IOCP wakes Uvicorn in constant time—completing four seconds of overlapping I/O in just two seconds.
